Studio is a React SPA configured with defineConfig(); each Studio workspace points at one project and dataset in the hosted Content Lake, reached through @sanity/client and real-time listeners. Cited for intent only.

Local mutations are applied optimistically and rebased onto remote mutations (rebase(), line 331).
Each document is a draft/published pair; publish, unpublish, discard and restore are pair operations.
Content Releases: release documents, version documents, release operations and plan limits.
Scheduled publishing uses Sanity's hosted Scheduling API, available on Growth or higher plans.

Image upload, crop and hotspot editing; asset uploads through the client adapter.
Reference picker with search and inline create.
Validation runs in the Studio, including checks on referenced documents.

Comments (and tasks, packages/sanity/src/core/tasks) live in a separate add-on dataset.
Presentation tool: visual editing of a front end with overlays and perspectives over postMessage.

GROQ playground plugin.
Content Lake stores any valid JSON document; schemas live in Studio configuration, not as database constraints; referential integrity between documents. Marketing page: cited for intent.

32 MB per document; 1,000 attributes per document (8,000 Enterprise); document quotas 10,000 Free / 25,000 Growth across datasets; listener connections live 4 hours; mutations 25 req/s per IP; 1,000 versions and 100 MB per release; 200 active releases per dataset.
Patches: set, setIfMissing, unset, insert, inc/dec, diffMatchPatch. Schema validation rules run only in Studio; API mutations are not checked against them.
Mutations grouped into transactions; all transactions recorded in a log served by the history API; queries run on a separate search store, so reads are eventually consistent.
History retention by plan: 3 days Free, 90 days Growth, 365 days Enterprise.
Drafts under drafts., versions under versions., published unprefixed; Content Releases group versions, preview, schedule and publish as a unit; paid feature.
Image pipeline transforms on the asset CDN by URL parameters; assets are public on the asset CDN even when the dataset is private.
GROQ-powered webhooks: GROQ filter and projection, before()/after() delta functions, retries for a plan-dependent period.

TapeDB capability catalog in this repository (release 0.4.2).

workloadAssumptions: One TapeDB workspace per dataset (site or environment); a CMS deployment holds several.
Editorial teams are small next to readers: tens of concurrent editors per workspace, millions of reads served from the delivery path, not the workspace.
Autosave writes are batched per document (on idle, about once a second at most), not per keystroke.
Documents stay well under Durable Object row limits (8 MB per value); large bodies are split into child rows.

architecture.summary: A compatible rewrite: a CMS layer on TapeDB, not a port of Content Lake. One TapeDB workspace per dataset holds documents, versions, releases, revisions and asset records with role and row rules; the Studio uses live queries, presence and the client outbox; assets are TapeDB files on R2 with transforms by the Images binding; published content is written to R2 and served behind the Workers Cache API by a delivery Worker refreshed from TapeDB webhooks; schedules run on Workflows. Everything deploys into the customer's own Cloudflare account.

capabilities.description: Datasets are isolated content environments
capabilities.candidate: One TapeDB workspace per dataset; claims are scoped to one workspace

capabilities.description: Several document changes commit together
capabilities.candidate: TapeDB $transaction in one workspace; optimistic locking by a rev column that every write must advance by one, enforced by a check() rule inside the transaction
capabilities.notes: Reads in Sanity are eventually consistent (separate search store); TapeDB reads see committed writes. Front ends written against Sanity may cache differently. Without the rev check, two concurrent publishes from one revision both land (negative control in examples/cms).

capabilities.description: Content types defined in code and compiled into storage
capabilities.candidate: A content-type language compiled to TapeDB models, a document and a draft model per type (examples/cms/cms/content.ts); migrations from tapedb migrate dev
gaps: Content Lake stores any JSON and has no migrations; here an added field is a generated migration file (no data-loss flag) to commit, and a removed field needs --accept-data-loss. The CMS still has to run migrate dev for the user.
The fixture covers string, slug, number, rich text and references; arrays of objects, images, files and localized fields are not compiled yet.
Arrays of objects with stable _key and deep nesting (20 levels in Sanity) have no direct column type: child models or t.json() decide what can be filtered.

capabilities.description: Validation of content rules
capabilities.candidate: check() write rules compiled from the content types: drafts may be incomplete but keep field constraints; a published document must be complete and valid
gaps: Sanity validates only in the Studio; here validation also runs on API writes, so an import can be refused where Sanity accepted the data (the importer must report it).
A check() rule sees only the row being written: rules that need other documents (a referenced document is published, a slug unique across drafts) cannot be checked there.

capabilities.description: References between documents with integrity
capabilities.candidate: belongsTo with onDelete restrict for strong references (to the target's document row); a plain indexed id column for weak ones
gaps: A strong reference points at the target's document row, which exists from the first draft: a document can be published while its referenced target is unpublished. Sanity refuses that; here it needs a check outside check() (it cannot read the target).
References into release versions need rules of the CMS's own.
Cross-dataset references are not supported: a relation stays in one workspace.

capabilities.description: Concurrent edits to one document merge at field and text level
capabilities.candidate: Whole-attribute writes; per-field locks on rich-text fields, enforced by check() rules (taken only when free, at most 30 s, released by the holder, taken over once expired); a CRDT (Yjs over broadcast) for rich text later
gaps: Measured: without a lock, two edits to one rich-text body from the same base lose one of them (last write wins on the attribute). Sanity applies path patches and diff-match-patch and rebases local changes, so both survive.
With locks no edit is lost, but editors take turns on a field; real co-editing of one field needs a CRDT or a sub-path patch operation (none on t.json() in TapeDB 0.4.2).
Lock expiry uses the Durable Object's clock against the client's requested term; a client clock far off can only shorten its own lock.
capabilities.notes: A sub-path patch operation for json attributes in TapeDB would close most of this; record it as a finding if the fixture confirms the gap.

capabilities.description: Editors and previews see changes as they happen
capabilities.candidate: TapeDB live queries over one socket per workspace
gaps: Sanity listeners emit mutation events (patches, transaction ids); live queries emit result diffs, so a Studio built on them diffs documents, not mutations.

Measured deployed: 20 editors autosaving once a second with 100 live queries, 600 saves in 30 s, none failed, p50 65 ms, p95 99 ms, p99 132 ms, max 226 ms from the client. Keystroke-rate saves were not measured; autosave stays batched.

capabilities.description: Who is looking at which document and field
capabilities.candidate: TapeDB presence rooms, field location in the presence payload
gaps: At most 4 presence rooms per socket by default; fan-out grows with the square of the room (60 ms p50 at 200 peers).

capabilities.description: A draft and a published version per document; publish, unpublish, discard, restore
capabilities.candidate: A document model (published values, rev, publishedAt) and a draft model sharing its id; publish writes the document and deletes the draft in one transaction; readers see published rows only (filter rule), drafts are for editors
gaps: Publish, unpublish, restore of an earlier revision and the refusal of a stale or invalid publish are tested; discarding a draft (deleting the draft row) is not.
Sanity's ID prefixes (drafts., versions.) become separate models; a query names the model, not a perspective.

capabilities.description: Group versions of many documents and publish them as a unit
capabilities.candidate: A cmsRelease model and a <type>Version model per type; publishing a release applies every version, writes their revisions, deletes the versions and marks the release published in one transaction
gaps: A release that spans datasets cannot be atomic: one workspace per transaction.

Measured locally only: 1,000 versions (3,001 writes) published whole in about 0.5 s under tapedb dev; not measured deployed, and no upper bound found (Sanity caps a release at 1,000 versions and 100 MB).
Scheduling a release (t.schedule), previewing a release as a perspective, and copying versions between releases are not built.

capabilities.description: Publish a document or release at a set time
capabilities.candidate: Workflows (sleepUntil the publish time, then call the publish route) or a Cron Trigger scanning due schedules
gaps: TapeDB provides no timers; the schedule is a row in the workspace and the timer lives in Workflows or a Cron Trigger.
A schedule changed after its workflow started must be detected at fire time (compare the schedule row's revision).

capabilities.description: Document revisions, restore, and who made each change
capabilities.candidate: An immutable <type>Revision row written in the same transaction as each publish and unpublish (values, rev, writer checked against the claim); restore copies a revision into the draft
gaps: Revisions are per publish, not per edit: Sanity also keeps every draft change; edit history of drafts is not recorded.
A check() rule cannot see other rows, so nothing in the engine forces a publish to carry its revision row: the CMS's publish route must (ops.ts does).
Sanity truncates history by plan (3/90/365 days); here revisions stay until an admin deletes them, and revisions holding personal data need personal fields to stay erasable.

capabilities.description: Upload, store and reference images and files
capabilities.candidate: TapeDB files on R2 with file rules; an asset record per file with metadata, crop and hotspot
gaps: Sanity's assets are public on its CDN even in private datasets; file rules here decide reads, so public delivery needs an explicit public rule or the delivery Worker.
Content-hash dedupe of uploads and image metadata extraction (dimensions, palette, blurhash) are application code.

capabilities.description: Resize, crop, format and hotspot-aware image URLs
capabilities.candidate: GET /img: the original read through TapeDB's file route as a reader (file rules: only public/ is served), transformed by the Images binding (fit cover, gravity at the focal point), cached with the Workers Cache API
gaps: Not verified deployed: this account is on legacy Image Resizing billing, so the binding refused every transform (IMAGES_TRANSFORM_ERROR 9432). Switching the account to an Images plan is the owner's decision.
Locally (wrangler's offline binding) resize, formats, caching and the public/ rule pass; the offline binding ignores gravity, so focal-point crops are asserted only deployed.
Parameter names differ from Sanity's image URLs; a compatibility layer for @sanity/image-url URLs is optional.
Billed per unique transformation beyond 5,000 a month.

capabilities.description: Front ends query published content
capabilities.candidate: A typed delivery SDK over TapeDB reads (findMany, include, aggregates), and named read-only SQL for one-off reads
gaps: No GROQ. Queries written for Sanity must be rewritten; projections become select/include.
Every engine route needs a verified claim: anonymous front-end reads go through the delivery Worker, not the workspace.

capabilities.description: Cached, high-volume reads of published content
capabilities.candidate: Signed TapeDB webhooks to the CMS Worker's own /_cms/hook (global_fetch_strictly_public) write each published document to R2, ordered by rev with unpublish tombstones; GET /content serves it through the Workers Cache API (max-age 10 s)
gaps: Measured deployed: a publish reached the delivery URL in 3.5 s and a republish in 2.8 s (new URLs); an unpublish of an already cached URL took 10.9 s, because the webhook's cache.delete runs in another data center than the reader's, so a cached URL changes only when max-age expires.
Global invalidation (a zone purge or cache tags) needs a custom domain; on workers.dev, max-age is the bound.
Only document fields are delivered: references are ids, not expanded; no query endpoint beyond by id and by slug.

capabilities.description: Notify other systems when content changes
capabilities.candidate: TapeDB signed change webhooks, filtered and shaped by the CMS before forwarding
gaps: No GROQ filters or projections; filtering is configuration of the CMS (type, perspective, fields).
Before/after values: what the TapeDB event body carries was not checked here.

capabilities.description: Find documents by text in the Studio and on sites
capabilities.candidate: TapeDB vector, text and hybrid search on one search-document model fed on save and publish
gaps: One indexed model per deployment: all content types share one search model.
The keyword half needs an embed provider; Vectorize visibility lags the write; no live search subscriptions.

capabilities.description: Members and roles decide who can read, edit and publish
capabilities.candidate: TapeDB role levels in compiled rules: users read published documents; members write drafts and release versions; editors publish; admins delete
gaps: Four fixed levels; Sanity's custom roles and document-level grant filters (per type or per field) are not mapped.
Under tapedb dev the role comes from the development claim; a deployment needs an identity adapter or built-in auth to assign it.

capabilities.description: Editors sign in
capabilities.candidate: TapeDB built-in auth (Better Auth) with the Studio on the same Worker
gaps: Sanity accounts and SSO are hosted by Sanity; SAML is out of TapeDB's scope.

capabilities.description: Export a dataset and import it elsewhere, including from Sanity
capabilities.candidate: TapeDB NDJSON export/import between workspaces; a Sanity importer that reads a datasets export tarball, maps documents to models and uploads assets to R2
gaps: TapeDB import copies file metadata, not file bytes; assets are copied separately.
The Sanity importer does not exist: Portable Text, references, drafts and versions must be mapped, and documents that fail server validation reported.

capabilities.description: An editing Studio generated from content types, extensible with plugins
capabilities.candidate: A new React Studio served from the user's Worker: generated forms, document lists, TipTap (ProseMirror) rich text, reference picker, image crop and hotspot, draft/publish bar, plugin API
gaps: Not built; the largest part of the product.
Adapting Sanity Studio itself (MIT) is not the proposed route: it is built around @sanity/client, Content Lake listeners and mutations (d.studio).
Rich text stored as ProseMirror JSON, not Portable Text: imports convert, and Sanity front-end renderers do not apply.

capabilities.description: Comments on fields and editorial tasks
capabilities.candidate: TapeDB models in the content workspace with live queries
gaps: Deferred past v1.

capabilities.description: Edit content in place on the live front end
capabilities.candidate: Preview mode in the framework integrations; overlays later
gaps: Deferred past v1; v1 has preview of drafts only.

capabilities.description: Canvas, Media Library, content variants and agent features
capabilities.candidate: None
gaps: Hosted Sanity services outside this assessment.

risks.description: Two editors in one rich-text body overwrite each other: TapeDB writes whole attributes.
risks.mitigation: Presence-based field locks in v1; measure with t.concurrent-edit; then a CRDT over broadcast or a json sub-path patch in TapeDB.

risks.description: All editors and autosaves of a dataset go through one writer; latency rises past about 4 concurrent writers.
risks.mitigation: Batch autosave; measure with t.autosave-load; split large organisations into several datasets.

risks.description: The Studio is the product and the largest piece of work; a thin Studio loses against Sanity's.
risks.mitigation: v1 scope fixed (content types, drafts and publishing, Studio, assets, delivery, SDK); plugin API from the start.

risks.description: Published content reaches the delivery path only after webhooks, which wait for the R2 flush (up to about 30 s).
risks.mitigation: Measure in t.delivery-snapshot; if too slow, have the publish route write the snapshot directly after commit and keep the webhook as the repair path.

risks.description: One indexed model per deployment limits search to one shared model.
risks.mitigation: A search-document model fed on save and publish; search marked optional.

risks.description: Sanity datasets may hold documents that break this CMS's server-side validation or use Portable Text features without a ProseMirror equivalent.
risks.mitigation: The importer reports per document and keeps unconvertible blocks as raw JSON for manual review.

costAssumptions.assumption: Editing traffic only (saves, live re-runs, presence); reads by readers go to the delivery path. Not modelled yet.
First 5,000 unique transformations a month included, then $0.50 per 1,000; a site with 2,000 images in 4 sizes is about 8,000 unique transformations, about $1.50 a month.

costAssumptions.driver: R2 storage and operations for assets and published snapshots

decisions.title: Compile content types into TapeDB models
decisions.context: Content Lake is schemaless JSON with schemas in Studio config; TapeDB is relational with reviewed migrations.

options.name: Compile content types into TapeDB models
options.tradeoffs: Types, foreign keys, filters and row rules per field; every model change is a migration the CMS must generate.

options.name: One generic documents model with a t.json() body
options.tradeoffs: Schemaless like Sanity, no migrations; no filtering or rules on fields inside the body, no foreign keys.

decisions.choice: Compile content types into TapeDB models
decisions.consequences: The CMS generates migrations for additive changes and asks for review of destructive ones (t.fixture-content-model, passing).

decisions.title: Build a new Studio rather than adapt Sanity Studio
decisions.context: Sanity Studio is MIT, but its document store, history, presence and search are written against Content Lake through @sanity/client and the mutator.

options.name: Adapt Sanity Studio to a TapeDB backend
options.tradeoffs: Mature UI for free; an adapter would have to emulate Content Lake's listeners, mutations, GROQ and history, which TapeDB does not provide.

options.name: A new Studio on TapeDB's client
options.tradeoffs: Large build; designed around live queries, presence and the outbox instead of emulating Content Lake.

decisions.choice: A new Studio on TapeDB's client
decisions.consequences: No Sanity code copied unless attributed under MIT; Sanity's form and structure concepts inform the design.

decisions.title: Rich text editor
decisions.context: Sanity stores rich text as Portable Text, edited with @portabletext/editor.

options.name: TipTap (ProseMirror)
options.tradeoffs: Mature, structured JSON documents, Yjs collaboration support; not Portable Text, so imports convert.

options.name: @portabletext/editor
options.tradeoffs: Sanity-compatible data; its license and coupling to Sanity packages were not checked.

options.name: Lexical
options.tradeoffs: Fast, Meta-maintained; its own JSON format, collaboration through Yjs as well.

decisions.consequences: The Sanity importer converts Portable Text to ProseMirror JSON; the SDK ships renderers.

decisions.title: Concurrent editing in v1
decisions.context: Sanity merges concurrent edits with path patches and rebasing; TapeDB writes whole attributes.

options.name: Presence-based field locks
options.tradeoffs: Simple, uses TapeDB presence; editors wait for each other on one field.

options.name: CRDT (Yjs) over TapeDB broadcast, persisted on save
options.tradeoffs: Real co-editing in rich text; more code and a second representation of the document while editing.

options.name: A json sub-path patch operation in TapeDB
options.tradeoffs: Closest to Sanity's model; a TapeDB core change with its own review.

decisions.consequences: v1 prevents silent overwrites (t.concurrent-edit, passing); co-editing of one field is the next step.

decisions.title: Serve published content from R2 and the Workers Cache API
decisions.context: A workspace has one writer and every engine route needs a claim; front ends need anonymous, cached reads.

options.name: Front ends read the workspace directly
options.tradeoffs: Always current; every reader is a Durable Object request and needs a claim.

options.name: Published snapshot in R2 behind the Workers Cache API
options.tradeoffs: Scales with readers and costs little; publish-to-live latency bounded by webhook delivery.

options.name: Published snapshot in Workers KV
options.tradeoffs: Fast reads; eventually consistent writes and a second store; KV is not required here.

decisions.choice: Published snapshot in R2 behind the Workers Cache API
decisions.consequences: The delivery Worker owns the snapshot format and its idempotent refresh.

decisions.title: Workflows for scheduled publishing
decisions.context: TapeDB has no timers; Sanity uses its hosted Scheduling API.

options.name: A Workflow per schedule (sleep until, then publish)
options.tradeoffs: Exact times, durable steps; a changed schedule must be checked at fire time.

options.name: A Cron Trigger every minute scanning due schedules
options.tradeoffs: One mechanism, minute granularity; scans every workspace with schedules.

decisions.choice: A Workflow per schedule (sleep until, then publish)
decisions.consequences: The schedule row carries a revision; the workflow publishes only if it still matches.

Content types compile to document and draft models; server-side validation refuses an incomplete or invalid publish, also sent straight at the model; published slugs unique; a strong reference refuses the target's deletion, a weak one may dangle; an added field generates a migration with no data-loss flag, a removal needs one

Readers see nothing until publish, then the whole document, live as one change; of two publishes from one revision exactly one lands; a publish on an older revision is refused and leaves draft and document as they were; an invalid publish rolls back whole; unpublish

A release publishes new and existing documents across types at once (a live reader never sees half); one document changed after the release was read, or one invalid version, refuses the whole release; of two concurrent publishes one lands and the release cannot be reopened; 1,000 versions publish whole (about 0.5 s locally)

Different fields written at once both land; without a lock one of two body edits is lost; with locks the second editor is refused until release and no edit is lost; four editors race for one lock and one gets it; an expired lock is taken over; a lock longer than 30 s is refused
20 editors autosaving once a second for 30 s with 100 live queries: every save lands (600, none failed); p50 65 ms, p95 99 ms, p99 132 ms, max 226 ms

Each publish and unpublish leaves a revision with values, rev and writer; a refused publish leaves none; revisions cannot be edited or written in another's name; restoring an earlier revision and publishing it makes a new revision
A scheduled release publishes at its time; a schedule changed after start does not fire the old version

Publish reaches the delivery path by id and slug (3.5 s deployed, 1.1 s under tapedb dev); a slug change and unpublish follow; cached reads hit; unsigned, wrongly signed and 5-minute-old deliveries refused; a late delivery of an older revision changes nothing
Resize, focal-point crop, WebP by default, cache hit on repeat, private files not served; deployed run refused by the account's legacy Image Resizing billing (IMAGES_TRANSFORM_ERROR 9432)

verdict.summary: A CMS with code-defined content types, drafts, atomic publish and releases, roles, live co-editing with presence, revisions, assets and cached delivery runs on TapeDB and Cloudflare in the customer's own account, with no server. It is a compatible rewrite, not a port of Content Lake: no GROQ, whole-attribute writes with field locks instead of path patches, and a new Studio. Image transforms need the account on an Images plan; scheduling and search are designed but untested.
excluded: Hosted add-ons (Canvas, Media Library, content variants, agent features): not part of the open-source product; no equivalent planned.
Comments and tasks: deferred past v1; buildable later as TapeDB models with live queries.
Visual editing overlays: deferred past v1; v1 previews drafts only.
GROQ: front ends use the typed delivery SDK; queries written for Sanity are rewritten.
